Chapter 1: Growing Up in a Town Shaped by Coal and Dreams.
Imagine living in the heart of a small Appalachian town, where life moves to the steady rhythm of the coal mine. The place is called Coalwood—and that name says it all. Pretty much every family counts on the mine. For most kids, the future feels decided before they’ve even had a chance to dream up something different. The air’s heavy with coal dust, and the constant hum of machinery echoes through the hills. For a lot of people, the mine isn't just a job—it’s a source of pride, but also a weight that gets handed down from one generation to the next. Fathers and sons, working side by side, their lives tightly bound to the earth beneath their boots. Now, picture a boy growing up here, watching his dad—who happens to be the mine superintendent—carry this huge load of responsibility for hundreds of men. The father’s days are long, his choices tough, and his hopes for his kids are shaped by the hard realities of Coalwood. Security is everything, and even with all its dangers, the mine offers just that. But the boy’s mother? She sees more. She wants her children to find a life that isn’t buried in the shadows of the mine—to reach for something brighter, maybe even safer. School becomes a fork in the road for a lot of kids in Coalwood. Some see it as a ticket out, a chance for something better. Others? It’s just a quick stop before heading underground. Teachers do their best to spark curiosity, but breaking through that wall of tradition isn’t easy. Most boys expect to follow their dads into the mine, and hardly anyone ever questions it.
Then, the world starts to change. News trickles in—stories about satellites orbiting the earth and rockets blasting into the sky. Even in this tiny town, those stories catch fire in a few teenagers’ imaginations. Suddenly, the idea that someone from Coalwood could build something that soars above the clouds doesn’t seem so crazy. The dream starts to take root. One boy in particular finds himself pulled in two directions. He respects his dad’s strength and commitment, but he’s drawn to science—and the promise of space. That tug-of-war between family expectations and his own ambitions quietly shapes his days and fills his mind with possibility. And he’s not alone. His friends, each carrying their own set of worries and hopes, start gathering after school. Their conversations drift from homework to rockets, from routine to wonder.
Those first rocket experiments? They’re rough. Clumsy, even. Scrap metal, borrowed chemicals, and whatever tools they can get their hands on—this is their toolkit. Backyards turn into makeshift labs, and every little success feels like a hard-won victory. Sure, the neighbors are skeptical. Some adults outright oppose what they’re doing, thinking it’s foolish or even dangerous. But every setback just makes the boys more determined. In the evenings, the boy’s mother stands at the kitchen window, watching. Her heart’s caught between worry and a quiet pride. She knows the risks, but she also sees a spark in her son’s eyes—a spark she hasn’t seen before. His father? He keeps his distance. Approval is hard to come by, and love shows up more in action than in words.
As time passes and seasons change, those rockets start to climb higher. Each launch draws a few more onlookers, and word spreads around town. People start to wonder—could these kids really pull off something extraordinary? The journey’s just beginning, but one thing is already clear: in a place where the future used to seem set in stone, a handful of dreamers are learning how to look up.
